name: Dana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Dana. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential and won't carry your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Great, I'm happy to. I love this stuff, to be honest, I've been reading about AI and farming for ages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Ruth Okafor at Hollow Lane, a small mixed farm with eighty ewes, about six hundred free-range hens and three acres of vegetables for a box scheme. Mornings are hens: let them out, collect and grade the eggs, check for red mite. Afternoons are sheep or veg, depending on the season, and twice a week I pack the veg boxes. I've only been farming two years, so I still make daft mistakes, like last month when I left a gate open and the ewes ate the kale.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI come into your day, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, actually. I use an AI assistant to plan the box contents from what's ready, to answer customer emails, and to write Ruth's little newsletter. Ruth hates screens, so she's happy I do it. The pay's still rubbish though, I share a house in town with two friends, Jo and Sam, and I've got about a fortnight of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was expecting more from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, well, that was overhyped, but at least the box scheme runs smoother. At work I'd tell Ruth the assistant still saves me an hour a day on emails. I'd still be the one telling everyone at the growers' meetup to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the same life as now, which is fine but tight. The work's secure, Ruth isn't going anywhere, but I'm on low pay with no savings and rent going up. The AI never was going to fix my wages, only my workload.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and use the extra hour to grow the box scheme, maybe from forty boxes to sixty. I'd ask Ruth for a small cut of any new box customers I bring in. And I'd keep going to the landworkers' alliance meetings in the city, because that's where people talk about pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. Safe-ish, but stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is rubbish. What does that mean week to week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't buy anything that isn't food, rent or diesel. My phone screen's been cracked since spring. If the van needed a new clutch, I'd have to borrow from my dad, which I hate doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruth agree to a cut of new box customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I showed her the numbers. She's fair but cautious, she remembers when the farm nearly went under in a bad year. I'd make a spreadsheet with the AI and put it in front of her over tea.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, but it still makes the box scheme smoother.
I'd keep telling the **growers' meetup** to try the tools anyway.
think: My job's **secure**, because Ruth isn't going anywhere.
My **pay and savings** stay tight while the rent keeps going up.
do: Use the saved hour to grow the box scheme to **sixty boxes**.
Ask Ruth for a **small cut** of new box customers.
Keep going to the **landworkers' alliance** meetings.
S0.quote: AI never was going to fix my wages, only my workload.
fieldNote: Dana is already a **daily AI user** and disappointed by the plateau.
Her worry is **low pay**, not job security, since Ruth relies on her.
She'd use the time saved to **grow the box scheme** and ask for a share.

steps.text: Keep running the hens and veg boxes at Hollow Lane
Use AI to grow the box scheme from forty to sixty boxes
Attend the landworkers' alliance pay meetings in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, booking, answering customers. That's literally half my desk time, so I'd feel this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is good if the gains are shared and awful if they aren't. I'd post about small farms getting cheap AI and robots through co-ops, not just the big estates. At work I'd show Ruth what the newer tools can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my email and planning job shrinks to nothing, but that was never what Ruth pays me for. The hands-on stuff, hens and sheep, stays mine for a good while because robots come slowly. If anything, I'd be more useful because I'd be the one setting the tools up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a short online course on farm robotics, the free one the agricultural college runs. I'd look into a shared egg-grading machine with two other small farms near us. And I'd keep saving whatever I can, maybe twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy. I'd be a junior farmhand in a world that suddenly wants what I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be more useful. What if Ruth decides the tools mean she needs fewer hours from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that worries me. Ruth counts every penny, and if the box scheme runs itself she might drop me to four days. I'd fight that by bringing in new work, like more boxes or a farm shop stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete, who helps Ruth at lambing. He doesn't use a phone, and if the farm moves to sensors on the ewes he'd feel pushed out. I'd want to teach him, but he'd hate being taught by a kid.

say: I'd say the change is good only if **gains are shared**.
I'd push for small farms to get **robots through co-ops**.
think: My **email and planning** tasks shrink, but they're not my real job.
Hands-on work with **hens and sheep** stays mine for a while.
do: Sign up for the free **farm robotics course** online.
Look into a **shared egg-grading machine** with two nearby farms.
Save about **twenty a week** where I can.
feel: Worried Ruth might cut me to **four days**.
S1.quote: I'd be a junior farmhand in a world that suddenly wants what I already know.
fieldNote: Dana sees the **thinking-task shift** as low risk for her hands-on role.
She'd push for a **shared machine** with neighbours, a co-op instinct.
Her hidden worry is **reduced hours** if the box scheme runs itself.

steps.text: Take the agricultural college's free online farm robotics course
Price a shared egg-grading machine with two nearby farms
Save twenty pounds a week from wages
Propose a small-farm machinery co-op at the growers' meetup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoa. Two years for AGI, five for the robots. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public ownership of some of this, or co-ops, straight away, before the big companies own every farm robot. I'd say it everywhere, the alliance, online, to Ruth's customers in the newsletter. A basic income would have to be part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side of Hollow Lane gets done by AGI in 2028, which I already half do with AI anyway. Then robots in 2031 could do the hens and the veg. I'd have about three years to become the person who runs those robots, or I'm out of work in a place with no other farm jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Ruth to let me trial the first affordable farm robots on the veg beds, so I'm learning them before they're everywhere. I'd do a proper robotics maintenance course, evenings, even if it costs money I haven't got. And I'd help start a co-op of small farms to share the machines and one operator, which would be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and fired up at the same time. It's like the first day of lambing, terrifying but you can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between AGI and the robots. What does that time mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. Ruth's farm would still need hands for those three years, so I'd keep earning while I learn. If I'm good at the robots by 2031, I'm the one the co-op hires, and if I'm not, I'm the one it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The course costs money you haven't got. How would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth to cover half, since she'd benefit. I'd sell my old guitar and stop going to gigs with Jo and Sam. If it came to it I'd borrow from my dad, though I'd hate it.

say: I'd say we need **co-ops or public ownership** of farm robots now.
I'd say a **basic income** has to be part of it.
think: AGI in 2028 takes the **thinking side**, which I half do already.
I'd have **three years** to become the person who runs the robots.
do: Get Ruth to **trial farm robots** on the veg beds early.
Help start a **small-farm co-op** with me as operator.
feel: **Nervous and fired up** together, like the first day of lambing.
S2.quote: If I'm good at the robots by 2031, I'm the one the co-op hires, and if I'm not, I'm the one it doesn't.
fieldNote: Dana treats the **three-year gap** as a learning window while still earning.
She'd **automate her own work** early to stay ahead of it.
Her blame and fix are **structural**: co-ops, public ownership and basic income.

steps.text: Persuade Ruth to trial a weeding robot on the veg beds
Take an evening robotics maintenance course, half paid by Ruth
Set up a machine-sharing co-op with nearby small farms
Campaign in the newsletter for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then 2034 for robots. Okay, that's more like a plan than a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things about co-ops and a basic income, but calmer. I'd say there's time to do it properly if councils and the government move now. I'd probably run a workshop at the growers' meetup on getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years before robots means I could build the co-op slowly and properly. I'd be thirty-five, with real experience. The risk is that the big estates move faster than us small farms and the co-op never gets off the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics course next year and keep doing it part time. I'd set up the co-op as a proper group with the two nearby farms in the first couple of years. And I'd start a little side business setting up AI planning tools for other small growers, maybe fifty pounds a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, honestly, with a worried bit underneath about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty pounds a farm. How many farms would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are maybe a dozen small growers within an hour of us. If half of them paid me fifty, that's three hundred pounds, which would double my savings. It's not much, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth about her own future here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's sixty, so by 2034 she'll want to step back. I'd ask whether she'd let the co-op run the farm with me as manager. Ruth (the farmer) would either love the idea of a co-op running Hollow Lane or throw a bucket at me.

say: I'd say there's **time** to do it **properly** if councils move now.
I'd run a **workshop** at the growers' meetup on getting ready.
think: Eight years lets me build the **co-op slowly** and properly.
The risk is **big estates** moving faster than small farms.
do: Start the **robotics course** part time next year.
Set up the **co-op** formally within two years.
Charge small growers **fifty pounds** to set up AI planning tools.
S3.quote: Ruth (the farmer) would either love the idea of a co-op running Hollow Lane or throw a bucket at me.
fieldNote: Dana uses five years to build a **side income** from her AI skills.
She imagines **managing the farm** as a co-op when Ruth retires.
Her worry is **competition** from big estates, plus her thin savings.

steps.text: Start a part-time robotics course next year
Register a machine-sharing co-op with two nearby farms
Charge small growers fifty pounds to set up AI planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade, and robots in 2039. That's almost a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we should all be hoping for, and we should use the time well. I'd say farmers shouldn't wait for the government but the government should help. I'd be loud about co-ops still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, probably. I'd have years to build skills and a client list. The only thing that scares me is the money in the meantime, because I've got a fortnight saved and that's a long decade on low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the side business slowly and do one course a year. I'd save properly, maybe a set amount each month into a separate account. I'd keep working at Hollow Lane and help Ruth plan for when she retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. Like a long walk up a hill you can actually see the top of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a decade change your view on the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make it more realistic. We could start small, share a hedge cutter or the egg grader, and build up trust. People round here need years to trust anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends Jo and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo works in a call centre and Sam does accounts, so honestly they're more at risk than me. I'd tell Jo and Sam (her housemates) to start learning a hands-on trade now, while there's a decade to do it.

say: I'd say this is the version to **hope for**, and we must use the time well.
I'd keep being loud about **co-ops** for small farms.
think: I'd probably be **fine** with years to build skills and clients.
My **fortnight of savings** makes a long decade on low pay scary.
do: Grow the **side business** slowly while working at Hollow Lane.
Save a **set amount** monthly into a separate account.
feel: **Uneasy but optimistic**, like a hill with a visible top.
S4.quote: I'd tell Jo and Sam (her housemates) to start learning a hands-on trade now, while there's a decade to do it.
fieldNote: With a decade, Dana's worry shifts to **low pay over time**, not job loss.
She notes her **desk-job friends** are more exposed than she is.
She'd build trust in the co-op slowly by **sharing small machines** first.

steps.text: Grow the AI setup service for small growers slowly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to get good at robots with no money behind me. What would help is cheap or free robotics training for farm workers, and some public money to help small farms buy machines together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the robots. That's the whole thing, really. If farm workers own a share of the machines, the robots are a gift, and if they don't, the robots take our jobs.

headlineQuote: If farm workers own a share of the machines, the robots are a gift, and if they don't, the robots take our jobs.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old farm worker** at Hollow Lane, a small hens, sheep and veg-box farm.
She uses **AI daily** for box planning and customer emails, and is keen on new tools.
Her plan in most pictures is to **become the robot operator** for a small-farm co-op.
She blames **ownership**, not technology, and wants co-ops and a basic income.
Her mood is **uneasy to anxious**, driven by thin savings rather than fear of change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only three years to learn robots and no money behind her.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for small farms to **share machines**.
